newsitem.title: USA: Should fund investors ride out next market drop?.
newsitem.headline: Should fund investors ride out next market drop?.

text.p: The average stock fund has gained 19.1 percent since the beginning of 1996. But rather than rejoice over their profits, many fund investors are worrying about how they can hold onto them.

Should you take your profits now and put them safely in a bank account or money market fund? Not according to most financial advisers, who insist that investors should hang onto their stock and bond funds through thick and thin.

Some investors find that advice hard to swallow, let alone follow. Others resolve to stick with their funds for the long term, but then panic and sell at the first sign of a downturn. In fact, you may be wondering how you will behave in the next bear market or market correction.
There are two ways to improve your chances of doing the right thing:
First, find out all you can about how the financial markets behave over time. Then you can make decisions based on the facts -- and not on your fears.

Here's one fact to keep in mind: short-term market moves don't affect long-term goals. Funds that invest in stocks are likely to suffer wider price swings than cash or fixed-income investments such as bond funds. But that doesn't matter in the long run. One recent study found that the stock market has gone up during 80 percent of all five-year periods and 85 percent of all 10-year periods since 1926.

Fact two: even a short absence from the stock market can be costly. Another study found that stocks delivered average annual returns of 14.8 percent from 1986 to 1995, a period of 2,526 trading days. But an investor who missed just the best 40 days in all that time would have earned only 2.5 percent annually. What's more, sometimes the best days come right after a sharp market decline.

The second thing to do is take a look at your investment plan. If you have a long time to go before you will need to draw upon your savings, you can easily afford to ride out fluctuations in the markets. Thus, you probably should invest the bulk of your assets in stock funds, which offer the best chance to stay ahead of inflation over long periods.

Be sure to combine funds that invest in different sectors of the equity markets, which tend to move in different cycles. That way, you won't be fully exposed to losses in a particular type of stock fund.

Most advisers suggest investing in a mix of small company funds, big company funds and international stock funds. Good choices in each sector include Fasciano Fund (800-848-6050; $1,000 minimum investment; no-load) for small company stocks; T. Rowe Price Blue Chip Growth (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum; no-load) for blue chips; and Hotchkis & Wiley International (800-346-7301; $5,000 minimum; no-load) for global issues.

That said, even aggressive investors shouldn't invest all their money in stock funds, which might expose them to truly frightening short-term losses. Such losses might cause even the best-informed investors to abandon their long-term plans and sell stock funds, perhaps when the market is at a bottom.

A better idea: Invest a significant stake -- at least 20 percent to 30 percent of your savings -- in more stable investments such as fixed-income funds. One first-rate candidate is John Hancock Strategic Income (800-225-5291; $1,000 minimum; 4.5 percent load).

The fund invests in several types of bonds, including U.S. Treasuries, high-yield corporate issues and bonds issued by foreign countries. Manager Frederick Cavanaugh has led the fund to a 9.2 percent annual return during the past five years, vs. 8.1 percent for the average multisector bond fund.

More conservative investors may prefer a fund that invests exclusively in bonds issued by the U.S. Treasury. One solid choice: Vanguard Fixed-Income Securities Fund Short-Term U.S. Treasury (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum; no-load).

The managers hold at least 85 percent of the fund's assets in Treasuries with the rest in bonds issued by government agencies. The fund has been only 60 percent as risky as the typical short-term government bond fund during the past five years.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
